clue.text: One is behind a religious superior in principle

indicators.note: says the piece for 'One' comes after the other pieces in the answer

parts.note: a prior is the superior of a religious house, ranking below an abbot
the Roman numeral for one is I

explanation.surface: A monk ranked below his prior, at least on paper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'is behind' puts I (one) after A and PRIOR.
explanation.definitionFit: A priori reasoning works from theory rather than observation, so it holds as a matter of principle.

clue.text: You'll get an offer on first month here in ivory coast

indicators.note: in a down clue, one piece placed on another sits above it, so it comes first

parts.note: the article 'an' gives the letter A
to bid is to make an offer, and a bid is an offer
January, abbreviated JAN, is the first month of the year

explanation.surface: Someone in West Africa is promised a deal at the start of the year.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on' puts A and BID above JAN in this down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: Abidjan is the largest city and economic capital of Côte d'Ivoire, the West African country.

clue.text: Memo sent around mid-may for the rest

indicators.note: the memo is placed round the middle letter of the month's name

parts.note: a memo is a note that jogs the memory, a reminder

indicators.note: mid- asks for the central letter of the word may

explanation.surface: An office note is circulated in mid-May telling everyone else what to do.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sent around' puts A, the middle of 'may', inside REMINDER.
explanation.definitionFit: The remainder is what is left over once part is gone: the residue.

clue.text: Month starts with Elgar and tippett for a small group

parts.note: OCT is the usual abbreviation for October

indicators.note: the starts of the two composers' names give their first letters

explanation.surface: A concert season opening with two English composers, programmed for chamber players.
explanation.walkthrough: Elgar and Tippett are English composers; only their initials E and T are used.
explanation.definitionFit: An octet is an ensemble of eight players or singers, a modest company.

clue.text: Foolish drinking is reckless

indicators.note: something drinking another takes it in, so the word for foolish contains the short form of is

parts.note: inane means silly or foolish
'is' can be shortened to 's, as in it's

explanation.surface: Someone is warning that drinking is dangerous behaviour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'drinking' puts S (from 's, short for 'is') inside INANE. 'Foolish' looks like the definition, but it is the outer piece.
explanation.definitionFit: An insane plan or risk is one taken with wild disregard for safety, i.e. madly rash.

clue.text: Indian city is seen in obscure drawing

indicators.note: one piece is found inside the other, here the city within the word for obscure

parts.note: dim means faint or obscure
Agra is the Indian city that is home to the Taj Mahal

explanation.surface: A city in India can be made out in a murky sketch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'is seen in' signals the container; 'obscure' looks like an adjective on the drawing, but it supplies the outer word.
explanation.definitionFit: A diagram is a simple drawing showing how something works or is arranged.

clue.text: Ballet performers represented as under strain initially

indicators.note: represented means presented afresh, so these letters are rearranged
initially asks for the first letter of strain

explanation.surface: Dancers are portrayed as struggling under stress.
explanation.walkthrough: 'represented' rearranges AS UNDER into DANSEUR; 'initially' adds S from 'strain'.
explanation.definitionFit: A danseur is a male ballet dancer, the French word used in ballet.

clue.text: One on cue with wine and starters in Rome

indicators.note: in a down clue, one piece placed on another sits above it

parts.note: an means one, as in an apple
a tip, or tip-off, is a hint or cue
Asti is a sparkling Italian wine from Piedmont

explanation.surface: A snooker player with a glass of wine before an Italian meal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on' puts AN above TIP. 'cue' suggests snooker, but here it means a hint.
explanation.definitionFit: Antipasti are the appetizers served at the start of an Italian meal, before the pasta.

clue.text: Talk endlessly with religious leader

indicators.note: endlessly means the word for talk loses its final letter

parts.note: to rabbit (on) is British slang for talking at length

explanation.surface: Chatting on and on with a cleric.
explanation.walkthrough: 'endlessly' drops the T from RABBIT. 'Rabbit' (on) is British slang for chattering.
explanation.definitionFit: A rabbi is a Jewish scholar and teacher who leads a congregation.

clue.text: I acted to acclaim once, ultimately 'twas me bust!

indicators.note: bust means broken, so these letters are smashed and reassembled
ultimately asks for the last letter of once

explanation.surface: A faded star admits her famous figure is what made her name.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ultimately' gives E from 'once'; 'bust' rearranges E with TWASME. The actress was famous for her curves, so 'bust' is a pun.
explanation.definitionFit: Mae West was a celebrated American stage and film actress of the 1930s, so she could say she performed to applause.

clue.text: Prisoners showing how chess games can end

definitions.meaning: games are finished when a king is trapped, so they end that way, split as two words

explanation.surface: Jailbirds pass their time playing chess to the finish.
explanation.walkthrough: Split as IN MATES, it describes games won by checkmate.
explanation.definitionFit: Inmates are those confined in a prison; checkmate is how a chess game is won.

clue.text: Big noise, with which it's hard to play cards!

definitions.text: with which it's hard to play cards
definitions.meaning: split as two words, it means lacking any furniture to deal the cards on

explanation.surface: A loud important person makes a card game difficult.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Big noise' is slang for an important person. Split as NO TABLE, the answer says there is nowhere to lay the cards.
explanation.definitionFit: A notable is a person of distinction, a VIP; without a table a card game is awkward.

clue.text: Business partnership for butchers?

definitions.meaning: a venture undertaken by two or more firms together
butchers sell joints of meat, so their trade is a business in joints

explanation.surface: A shared venture suited to people who cut meat.
explanation.walkthrough: A joint is a cut of meat, so a butcher's business could whimsically be described this way.
explanation.definitionFit: A joint enterprise is a commercial project run jointly by partners; read whimsically it is a meat-joint business.

clue.text: Eve, perhaps, one who's barely seen

definitions.meaning: Eve in Eden wore no clothes, an example of the type
barely means without clothes, so someone seen unclothed

explanation.surface: The first woman, described as scarcely visible.
explanation.walkthrough: 'barely' looks like 'hardly', but here means 'without clothes'.
explanation.definitionFit: A nudist goes unclothed, as Eve did in the Garden of Eden.

clue.text: Hooker's overwhelmed by throw that's astonishing

indicators.note: the prostitute is engulfed by the word for throw, so it goes inside

parts.note: to sling is to throw
hooker is slang for a prostitute, as is tart

explanation.surface: A rugby hooker is buried under a lineout throw, which is surprising.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hooker' suggests the rugby position, but here it is slang for a prostitute, and 'overwhelmed by' signals that it goes inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Something startling is so surprising it makes you jump.

clue.text: Explore likelihood of event taking place

definitions.meaning: to search an area for gold or minerals
a chance or expectation of something happening

explanation.surface: Investigate how probable something is.
explanation.definitionFit: To prospect is to search the ground for ore; a prospect is a chance of something coming about.

clue.text: English mad with certain artwork

parts.note: raving means wildly mad

explanation.surface: An English painter, crazy about one piece of art.
explanation.definitionFit: An engraving is a print made from an incised plate, one kind of art.

clue.text: "Political honours" always featuring in parts of the paper

indicators.note: featuring in means appearing inside, so the word for always goes within the pages

parts.note: a newspaper is made up of pages
e'er is the poetic short form of ever, meaning always

explanation.surface: Honours lists for politicians are always printed in the newspapers.
explanation.walkthrough: E'er is the poetic contraction of 'ever'; 'featuring in' signals the container.
explanation.definitionFit: Peerages, titles that bring a seat in the House of Lords, are often awarded to politicians.

clue.text: Relatively unproductive time perhaps in eg Dakar, capital of Senegal

indicators.note: perhaps signals the letters could be arranged another way
the capital letter, the first, of Senegal

explanation.surface: A slack period in Senegal's capital city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' rearranges EG DAKAR into DARKAGE; 'capital of' adds S. Dakar really is Senegal's capital, so 'capital' looks like geography.
explanation.definitionFit: The Dark Ages, roughly 500 to 1000 AD in Europe, are held to have been culturally barren.

clue.text: Various water birds seen on end of groyne

indicators.note: in a down clue, the birds sit above, so come before, the next letter

parts.note: divers are diving water birds, called loons in North America

indicators.note: end of asks for the last letter of groyne

explanation.surface: Several kinds of seabirds sit at the tip of a sea wall.
explanation.walkthrough: 'seen on' puts DIVERS above E, the last letter of 'groyne' (a low wall built out into the sea).
explanation.definitionFit: Diverse means varied or of many different kinds.

clue.text: After first and last characters swapped, Aussie is manipulated

indicators.note: the first letter and the last letter trade places with each other
points to the opening and closing letters of the word for Aussie

parts.note: digger is informal for an Australian, originally a soldier

explanation.surface: An Australian is cheated once things are switched round.
explanation.walkthrough: 'first and last characters swapped': DIGGER, with its first and last letters D and R exchanged, becomes RIGGED.
explanation.definitionFit: Something rigged, such as a vote, has been fixed dishonestly.

clue.text: Twenty four hours consuming canned pils in show

indicators.note: consuming means taking in, so the day contains the jumbled beer

parts.note: a day lasts twenty-four hours

indicators.note: canned is slang for drunk, so these letters are scrambled

explanation.surface: A whole day spent drinking cans of lager on show.
explanation.walkthrough: Pils is a pale lager, and 'canned' is slang for drunk, signalling its letters are jumbled; 'consuming' signals the container.
explanation.definitionFit: A display is an exhibition or show.

clue.text: Not Tintin's partner in dance!

parts.note: the comic-strip boy's name splits as tin tin; swap each tin for a synonym, a metal container, and the doubled word is a dance, not a companion

explanation.surface: The boy reporter is not part of a dancing couple.
explanation.walkthrough: Tintin's companion is the dog Snowy, but the trick is to read 'Tintin' as tin + tin and use the other word for a tin, giving the high-kicking Parisian dance.
explanation.definitionFit: The cancan is a lively high-kicking dance from Paris music halls; can is another word for tin.

clue.text: Is a gal besotted with meat never getting these?

definitions.text: Is a gal besotted with meat never getting these?

indicators.note: besotted means fuddled or infatuated, so these letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: A girl so averse to meat she only eats plant-based dishes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'besotted' rearranges ISAGAL and MEATNEVER. Read as a whole, the clue also describes the answer: food for someone who never eats meat.
explanation.definitionFit: Meat-free dishes are what someone who never eats meat would order.

clue.text: Bags of tears after finale in the ring

indicators.note: places the word for tears after the letter just found
the finale, the last letter, in the word ring

parts.note: rips are tears in cloth

explanation.surface: Boxers' handbags or grapples at the end of a bout.
explanation.walkthrough: 'finale in' takes G from 'ring'; 'after' puts RIPS after it. 'Bags' is a verb in the surface, but a noun here: grips are travel bags.
explanation.definitionFit: A grip is an old word for a travelling bag or holdall.

clue.text: Extra staff principally needed for customs

parts.note: more means additional or extra

indicators.note: principally means chiefly, so the first letter of staff

explanation.surface: More employees are needed at the border control.
explanation.walkthrough: 'principally' takes S from 'staff'. 'customs' suggests the border, but means traditions.
explanation.definitionFit: Mores are the customary conventions of a society.

clue.text: Using abusive language for a fence

definitions.meaning: to rail at someone is to scold them bitterly

explanation.surface: Someone shouting insults at a fence.
explanation.definitionFit: Railing against someone means ranting at them; a railing is a barrier of bars and posts.

clue.text: Di and carol drunk? Not on this!

definitions.text: Di and carol drunk? Not on this!

indicators.note: drunk means intoxicated and so jumbled, giving the letters a new arrangement

explanation.surface: Two friends, Di and Carol, couldn't get tipsy on this soft drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'drunk' rearranges DICAROL. Read as a whole, the clue also says you can't get intoxicated on it, since the drink is non-alcoholic.
explanation.definitionFit: Cordial is a sweet fruit syrup diluted with water, a soft drink.

clue.text: Sensing trouble with national standards

indicators.note: trouble means disturb, so these letters are disordered

explanation.surface: Feeling unease about the levels set for the whole country.
explanation.walkthrough: 'trouble' rearranges SENSING. 'standards' suggests benchmarks, but means flags.
explanation.definitionFit: Ensigns are flags; a standard is also a flag.

clue.text: One's thrown brightly coloured bunch of flowers

indicators.note: thrown means tossed about, so these letters are mixed up

parts.note: the letters of 'one's', counting the s
gay in its older sense means bright and cheerful in colour

explanation.surface: A bride throws her colourful bouquet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'thrown' rearranges ONES into NOSE; then add GAY in its old sense of bright.
explanation.definitionFit: A nosegay is a small posy of sweet-smelling blooms.
